references.text: In the preceding verse, the Lord gives the servant an order to go out and bring people in. Luke 14:21 is the direct command that the servant here in verse 22 reports has been carried out: 'Lord, it is done as you commanded.'

Since there is still room, the Lord sends the servant out once more in Luke 14:23 – now to the roads and paths – to fill the house. The servants' obedience and the fact that there is still space drive the action forward.
The parable of the great banquet begins in Luke 14:16–17, where a man sends his servant to invite guests. Verse 22 shows the servant's faithful report after completing the task.

In Matthew's parallel parable of the wedding feast, the king says that those invited were not worthy and sends his servants out to the crossroads to gather all they can find (Matthew 22:8–10). The same pattern: the original guests refused, and there is still room.

The servant does exactly what the Lord has commanded, reflecting the principle of obedience to the Lord's commands, as also expressed in the Great Commission: Matthew 28:20 – 'teach them to obey everything I have commanded you.'

Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles after the Jews reject the message (Acts 13:46–47). This reflects the pattern of the parable: when those first invited would not come, others were brought in, and there was still room.

Paul explains in Romans 11:11–12 that Israel's fall has meant salvation for the Gentiles. The parable in Luke 14 illustrates this: those originally invited refused, but there was still room, and others were invited in.

The invitation to come remains open: 'Let anyone who is thirsty come' (Revelation 22:17). That there is still room at the banquet in Luke 14:22 points forward to God's enduring and open invitation of grace.

Isaiah's invitation to all who are thirsty (Isaiah 55:1–2) forms the Old Testament background for the open invitation of the banquet. That there is still room emphasizes God's generous and inclusive call.
